cultivar: Varied by farm; Okumidori, Gokō and Asanoka among those sold singly
processing: Sencha is steamed and rolled in the usual way; a large and growing share of the town's leaf is shaded and made into tencha for matcha.
harvest_season: As with other Kyoto greens, the spring first flush is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Typically dark green sencha needles; tencha is flat, flaky and unrolled.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green for sencha, depth varying by cultivar and steaming.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf pieces, typical of sencha.
taste_profile: Varies by farm and cultivar, since the name covers each grower's own tea. Expect the green sweetness and savouriness usual for Kyoto sencha rather than one fixed flavour.

brewing.notes: Start at about 70°C for a single-cultivar sencha, then taste and adjust. Gokō is usually happier a little cooler and Asanoka takes slightly more heat.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year's spring crop, usually best within a year. Farm-direct lots name the grower and often the cultivar; most of the town's tea is not sold under its name at all and goes through wholesalers as Uji tea.
description:
Wazuka is the town in southern Kyoto that grows more Uji tea than anywhere else while hardly anyone knows its name. In fiscal 2014 it produced 1,101 of the prefecture's 2,711 tonnes, about 41%, yet most of it passes through wholesalers and is sold simply as Uji tea.

The town sits among steep hills with the Wazuka River running between them, big swings between day and night temperatures and frequent morning mist. Sencha is long established, but demand for matcha used in food processing has pushed tencha up sharply, from 250 tonnes in 2004 to 717 in 2015.

The name is a brand rather than a single style: from the late 2000s growers began selling their own teas directly, each differing with field, cultivar and farming choices. So compare farms, not just the label. Brew sencha cool and short at first, and let the second steep be quick.

Look for a named farm and cultivar: Okumidori, Gokō and Asanoka are all sold singly. If you visit, the hillside fields at Ishidera are the town's most photographed.
history:
Nobody knows exactly when tea growing started here; it is thought monks brought it some time after the start of the Kamakura period. In the Genbun era farmers tried selling to Uji tea merchants, more households took up tea as a side business, and by the Tenpō era sales reached about a thousand kin a year. After Yokohama opened in 1859 production grew again, with export trade flourishing in the Keiō years.

In the Meiji period the town's own account describes it as just one more mountain growing area, unremarkable for quality. By late Meiji it led the prefecture in volume, and some growers won prizes at the national industrial expositions of 1890 and 1895. Better fertilising, field and product competitions and machine processing later raised quality.

The modern brand came with farm-direct sales from the late 2000s. The Wazuka tea fields became the first area listed as a Kyoto Prefecture scenic asset on 24 January 2008, and a farmer-run tea café opened that June.
